paragraphs: Alabama, Florida and Indiana each carried out an execution on Thursday, according to The Guardian, in an unusual coincidence. It was the second time since August that three states were set to execute prisoners on a single day. Before this year, the last time it happened was 2010.

Florida executed Jesse Guardado by three-drug lethal injection, its record-tying 19th execution of the year. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman in her Walton county home in 2004 and taking her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. In Indiana, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12.45am. He had acknowledged killing his girlfriend's two children in a 2010 house fire. Alabama executed Michael Taylor, 54, who was convicted of beating two people, aged 83 and 79, to death during a 1991 robbery.

Several last-minute disputes were rejected. Taylor's attorneys objected to a switch to lethal injection after a judge declared the nitrogen gas method unconstitutional, since he had chosen nitrogen years ago, but a judge ruled against him. Weisheit's lawyers failed to persuade Governor Mike Braun to allow brain scans or to grant clemency. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey also declined to reduce Taylor's sentence. Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty said the state would be killing a mature man, not the 19-year-old who made a terrible mistake. Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita called Weisheit's execution long-awaited justice for the two children who died.

The same day, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced he would commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values. Florida, by contrast, has carried out more than half of the 34 US executions so far this year. The Guardian reports the death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny since the failed September execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, though courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions.

Pope Leo XIV is starting a 12-day trip to Latin America about three weeks after surgery for lung cancer, the BBC reports. The tour covers Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he spent many years as a priest. Leo himself revealed last month that doctors found a tumour during a routine scan. It was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung, and his medical team confirmed the cancer had not spread.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken. It described him as a 71-year-old who has undergone an operation, not someone with a permanent medical condition. A spokeswoman said he has fantastic stamina and personally confirmed the schedule with no changes. Villanova University's Professor Massimo Faggioli told the BBC the Vatican's message is that the illness was a short episode and the Pope is back on track. The trip involves multiple long-haul and local flights over thousands of miles.

Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen steeply, gets its first papal visit in four decades. In Argentina, the homeland of Pope Francis, the visit could be the most politically sensitive leg. The BBC notes President Javier Milei once called Francis "evil on earth" and a communist, while Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's austerity measures. Milei has nonetheless welcomed Leo, writing on X that Argentina awaits him with immense joy.

Peru comes last. Born in the US, Leo spent almost 20 years there, on and off, and holds Peruvian citizenship. He will visit Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014, then say Mass in Cusco and travel to Pucallpa in the Amazon. The Vatican says he will meet survivors of clerical sexual abuse in all three countries. Faggioli also raised the question of whether Leo will visit the United States while Donald Trump is president.

With 30-year fixed mortgage rates at 7% or more, some borrowers are reconsidering adjustable-rate mortgages, according to a report from NPR's The Indicator. ARMs are far less popular than fixed loans, making up only about 5% of US mortgages. The 30-year fixed loan dominates, and the US is described as the only country where it is the most popular kind of home loan.

An ARM starts with an introductory rate, usually a little lower than the prevailing fixed rate, and then resets to wherever the market is after a set period. NPR notes the loans carry painful memories. About a third of mortgages originated in the run-up to the housing bubble were ARMs, and predatory lenders pushed novel versions on people with low incomes and bad credit, approving them based only on the low teaser rate. Analysis from Duke found the delinquency rate for conventional ARMs was double that of fixed-rate mortgages at the peak of the subprime crisis. Regulators have since added safeguards, and borrowers now must qualify at a rate well above the teaser rate.

Redfin analyzed data going back to 1971 and asked whether a borrower who chose an ARM would have had a chance to refinance into a lower rate. About 70% of the time, they would have. Chen Zhao, head of economics at Rocket Mortgage and Redfin, said that suggests ARMs mostly made sense over that stretch. NPR noted fixed-rate borrowers could also have refinanced, but at additional cost.

The reporters gave two caveats. The long period of falling rates may have been a historical anomaly, and borrowers are human. Many homeowners want certainty about monthly payments and will pay a little extra for it, so the appeal of ARMs, they said, is not broad.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is urging UK businesses to publish salaries in job adverts now rather than wait for a law that would require it, the BBC reports. The government plans to make pay details compulsory and says legislation will come forward as soon as possible. It has said it will set out what information will be required and how the rules will be enforced in due course.

The government argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly first-time applicants, and could help prevent pay discrimination. It says upfront pay details could expose unjustified differences and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes. Burnham said people should know what a job pays before spending time applying. Treasury minister James Murray called it an important common sense reform. The government said a Cabinet Office consultation launched in the summer showed overwhelming support, with 94% of respondents backing greater transparency. It ties the move to efforts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training, ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review.

Industry views are mixed. Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said openness should be the norm and that adverts with salaries attract more and better-suited applicants. Adzuna data show 51% of its September adverts had salary information, a share that has been falling. The CIPD, a human resources body, said disclosure is good in principle but more complicated in practice because there is not always a single fixed figure. Its chief executive, Neil Carberry, said drafting adverts is best left to good employer practice rather than regulation.

A week earlier, the Equality and Human Rights Commission called publishing salaries a positive step. It also said employers should have to answer questions about colleagues' pay and should be barred from asking about current salary. The EU is introducing similar measures.

The polar vortex, the ring of strong winds that circles the Arctic each winter, has weakened and shifted in recent days, the BBC reports. It has stretched and briefly split into two smaller circulations. Scientists say such an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations. Some forecasts show the vortex winds reversing by mid-November, which would count as a major sudden stratospheric warming, or SSW.

Jeff Knight, a Met Office lead climate scientist, told the BBC it appears to be the earliest on record in 75 years of observations. The previous earliest major SSW events came on 28 November, in 1969 and 2025. The cause is unclear and could simply be natural variability. Knight suggested the current record El Niño may have helped load the dice, but said there is not enough evidence because the event is so rare.

In past years, SSW events have sometimes been followed by colder weather in parts of Europe and North America. They can increase the chance of blocked weather patterns that bring drier conditions and cold northerly or easterly winds, with a greater chance of snow in eastern UK. Met Office long-range forecasts had pointed to a stormy start to winter followed by a colder spell, in line with El Niño, and this early SSW was not widely expected.

Professor Andrew Perez-Charlton of the University of Reading said the typical response is colder and drier conditions, but that it is harder to anticipate a cold spell this time. The Arctic is not yet as cold as in midwinter, so any influence could be weaker and cold, snowy weather is far from guaranteed. His concern is a dry pattern, since most of England and Wales is still in drought and reservoirs are very low. Experts stress it is too early to know whether the winter outlook will change.

A federal judge has barred the Trump administration from doing any construction on the proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington for 14 days. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued the temporary restraining order around midnight Thursday into Friday. It came hours after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in an 8-4 vote. NPR reported that the administration had told the court it could begin excavation the same day.

Chutkan granted a request from the governments of Washington, D.C., and Virginia. Her order was consolidated with an earlier lawsuit by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. According to NPR, her 33-page opinion questioned the administration's shifting justifications for the arch and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed. She said traffic disruptions would begin as soon as construction does. Administration officials have said work would run 20 hours a day for two to three years.

The commission's hearing lasted about nine hours, and NPR said 131 people had signed up to speak. Most speakers opposed the arch. Chair Mark Paoletta, a Trump appointee, said the president understands the importance of grand monuments. D.C. council member Phil Mendelson, who sits on the panel, said Congress had neither approved the project nor appropriated money. Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat, called it illegal. NPR reported that supporters on the commission maintained Congress authorized the project through a 1925 approval of two columns on Memorial Circle that were never built.

The cost and funding remain unclear. The Guardian said some estimates reach $100 million. The administration's response to the ruling was not in the reports reviewed. The restraining order lasts 14 days, and the consolidated lawsuits continue.

Israel's President Isaac Herzog said he will name a candidate to form the next government by Sunday. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot received more recommendations from lawmakers than Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog spoke on Thursday after long consultations with the parties in the 120-seat Knesset. According to Al Jazeera, 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, and 46 backed Netanyahu.

Herzog said the results may appear clear, but "mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves" make it hard to say who is best placed to assemble a coalition. He plans personal talks with some party leaders over the weekend. The October 27 election left neither man with a clear path to a majority. Netanyahu's Likud won 27 seats, the most of any party, but his wider coalition won 53. Eisenkot's alliance of four Jewish-led parties won 48, and two parties representing Israel's Palestinian minority won 19.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out governing with the Arab-led parties, though both recommended him. Netanyahu also lost a possible backer when United Torah Judaism declined to recommend anyone. The Times of Israel reported the party broke with him over failed legislation to exempt ultra-Orthodox men from military service.

Netanyahu has cited an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results and accused Arab-led parties of stealing the vote. Critics say he is trying to undermine the outcome, which he denies. The Central Election Committee said the election's integrity was not compromised. Once Herzog picks, the nominee has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister meanwhile.

President Trump said a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be near after meeting Kirill Dmitriev, Vladimir Putin's special envoy, at the White House on Thursday. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, "I think we're going to be very close to settling Russia-Ukraine," but declined to describe his conversation with Dmitriev. He said an agreement would be big and would involve more than Ukraine, possibly "all of Europe." He said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation.

Al Jazeera noted that Trump has often predicted an agreement was close, though negotiations have picked up in recent weeks. NPR reported that the United States will lead a new round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

The meeting followed an event hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together. It marked a six-day local truce she helped broker in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in Ukraine's Kherson region. The truce ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians and deliveries of food and medical supplies. Attendees included Dmitriev and Ukrainian parliament figures David Arakhamia and Dmytro Lubinets. The president did not attend.

The White House called the event a diplomatic breakthrough, according to NPR, but some European analysts worry such efforts could backfire. Heather Conley of the American Enterprise Institute said the U.S. must be careful not to treat Russia and Ukraine as equals in the crisis. Dmitriev thanked the first lady on behalf of Putin, and Ukraine's Lubinets presented her with an award. No terms of a broader deal have been made public.

Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz, according to Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee. He told the Iranian Students' News Agency that ships from these countries "pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either." Iran effectively closed the strait early in the war with the United States and Israel, which began on February 28, and the U.S. reimposed a naval blockade on Iran's southern ports in July.

Hayat Moqaddam said Iran will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, and will collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships. Qatari vessels pass free, and he did not say whether Iraqi ships pay. Analysts told Al Jazeera that Iran may be seeking revenue and trying to weaken acceptance of Washington's strategy. Al Jazeera noted that Iran began letting ships from friendly countries pass within weeks of the war starting and exempted Iraq in April.

All four countries depend heavily on the strait. Kpler's Muyu Xu said about 42 percent of the Gulf crude passing through it in October went to China and 13 percent to India. Iran analyst Rouzbeh Parsi said the exemptions carry upsides but also political dangers for the countries involved.

Whether ships can get past the blockade depends on Washington. US Central Command has said it applies to all vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports, while ships avoiding those ports are unaffected. Analyst Wolfgang Pusztai said it is unclear whether "ships of these countries" refers to flag, owner or operator.

Iran appears to be carrying out significant new construction near at least two major missile sites and repairing other bases damaged by months of U.S. and Israeli air strikes, according to a BBC Verify analysis of satellite images. Analysts at the British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the November images, said they show digging and new buildings at the Garmdareh base in Karaj, near Tehran, and at the Shahroud base in the north.

At least 12 other military sites show signs of repair, the BBC reported. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base, and debris has been cleared at the Parchin complex. Analysts said construction appears largely complete at Parchin's Taleghan 2 facility, where an underground bunker was repaired and reinforced with concrete. Sam Lair of the Foreign Policy Research Institute said the Karaj images appear to show a new portal for an underground facility. MAIAR also identified excavations near tunnel entrances close to Qom.

Former CIA analyst Jim Lamson said the Shahroud digging could relate to missile production and that the Revolutionary Guards are probably trying to move production underground. A MAIAR analyst noted a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to survive strikes. Sean O'Connor of Janes said the work is unlikely to be a deception effort, which would be costly. Mark Cancian of CSIS said the purpose is probably to better defend against future attacks.

The findings contrast with U.S. claims. A Pentagon spokesperson said the U.S. had destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base, while Iran says it retains large stockpiles. Speculation has grown that the U.S. could resume strikes after the midterms.

Russian President Vladimir Putin met Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, in Moscow on Thursday to discuss regional security. According to Iran's state broadcaster Press TV, Rezaei delivered a letter from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. He did not say what the message contained. The Kremlin had not immediately released its own account, Al Jazeera reported.

Rezaei said the talks covered security arrangements for the post-war period, Russian support for ending what he called U.S. "aggression," and energy cooperation, including a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran. He said Putin repeated that Russia is ready to help end the war. He also said he briefed Putin on a late October meeting in Tehran among Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.

The meeting came as Qatar steps up diplomacy amid fears the U.S. could renew attacks after Tuesday's midterms, in which Republicans lost both chambers of Congress. Efforts to end the war center on the Strait of Hormuz, the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions and the nuclear program. Rezaei said Iran has announced seven conditions to the Americans and, until they are met, will neither reopen the strait nor negotiate. Khamenei said in a written statement on Wednesday that there should be no inclination toward submission to the U.S.

Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi phoned counterparts in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, Turkiye and Jordan, Iranian state media reported. Russia and Iran signed a strategic partnership treaty in 2025 that does not include a mutual defense clause. Iran's army spokesman said Iran has bought Russian Su-35 jets it expects after the war.

Vice President JD Vance privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war, according to an Axios report on November 4 that Fox News summarized. The remarks are secondhand, and Vance has not been quoted on the record saying this. Vance did write on X on Wednesday, "The reason we lost is the war," referring to Republican losses in Tuesday's midterms. The White House's response to the Axios report was not included in the Fox article.

Fox reported that Vance has led a faction of administration officials urging Trump to negotiate an end to the conflict. Netanyahu had urged Trump to resume strikes against Iran before the midterms, but Trump held off. Natan Sachs of the Middle East Institute told Fox that Vance's main concern appeared to be a Netanyahu plan for regime change. Sachs said that criticizing Netanyahu lets Vance distance himself from the administration without attacking Trump, and he called the 2028 presidential race effectively underway. Roughly six in 10 voters said military action against Iran was the wrong decision, according to the AP Voter Poll.

Vance has also been involved in diplomacy. According to Axios, he sent a letter last month through Qatari intermediaries to Mohsen Rezaei proposing renewed talks that must address Iran's nuclear program. A U.S. official said Trump backed it. Rezaei confirmed receiving it but said he had not responded.

The White House is weighing renewed strikes, continued economic and naval pressure, or a negotiated settlement. Reuters reported that Iran sent a formal nuclear proposal through Qatar, making talks contingent on its seven demands.

The White House has denied rumors that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs after Tuesday's Republican midterm losses. The BBC reported that the White House and State Department called reports about Rubio "fake news." Rubio told The New York Times that serving until the end of Trump's term has "always been my plan."

Hegseth faces more pressure. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for the losses, and some media reports have called for Hegseth's replacement over his handling of it. Trump told ABC News he had received "calls about" Hegseth but had "every intention" of keeping him, and later said Hegseth "has done a fantastic job." The Washington Post reported Trump may be considering removing Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine or Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper.

Republican Representative Thomas Massie said he will trigger a resolution to impeach Hegseth early next week and urged Trump to replace him before the new Democratic-controlled Congress forms in January. Hegseth, in a video, called the effort a "sham" by a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and his Democratic allies, and defended his record on recruitment and the defense industrial base.

The Washington Examiner, citing the Associated Press and Punchbowl News, reported that Senator Marsha Blackburn is not considering Hegseth to fill her Senate seat once she becomes Tennessee's governor in January. A source close to Blackburn called the speculation baseless.

President Trump blamed voters for a sharp stock market drop, writing on Truth Social on Thursday evening that the market crashed because Democrats "had a big Tuesday." He wrote, "So sad to see, you only have yourselves to blame!" In a second post he said the market suffered "one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election" and that Americans' 401(k)s had dropped. He added that the country would soon be "BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE."

The Washington Examiner reported that Democrats retook the House and Senate on Tuesday, reaching at least 253 House seats and at least 54 Senate seats, as voters responded to affordability messaging. The outlet said Thursday's selloffs were tied to losses in artificial intelligence-related stocks, a sharp contrast with a post-midterm surge on Wednesday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite fell more than 5 percent on Thursday.

The Examiner linked the selloff to investor worries about the future of the U.S. AI industry. It said many winning Democratic candidates, including Senator-elect Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, criticized the widespread expansion of data centers. It said data center moratoriums became increasingly popular with candidates in both parties, and that some officials, such as New York Governor Kathy Hochul, have already put them in place this year.
The article did not say whether Democratic leaders have responded to Trump's posts, and it offered no market figures beyond the Nasdaq decline.

Macau has sentenced Au Kam San, a 69-year-old former lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner, to 12 years and six months in jail in the city's first national security case, the BBC reported. Au was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences, after a closed-door trial.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state". Au was arrested in July 2025 and charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by contacting foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality. He was found guilty of four of the seven charges after a three-day trial that ended in September. A judge ordered the trial closed to ensure no prejudice to national security interests, and Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case.

Au's family had told the media that he was not allowed to seek his own lawyer and was assigned one by the court. His wife, Virginia Cheang, called the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au". In an open letter she said she hoped authorities would let her family write to and visit him regularly, adding: "I dare not hope for more."

Macau was handed back to China in 1999. Its national security law took effect in 2009 and was revised in 2023 to cover non-violent acts of secession, and again this year to allow closed-door trials. A former primary school teacher, Au was elected to the Legislative Assembly in 2001 and spent 20 years as one of a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers. He co-organised annual Tiananmen vigils, which have effectively been banned in Macau and Hong Kong since 2020.
The sentence came a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, 30, to 10 years in jail. Wong has been in custody for six years.

Turkey's parliament has ratified a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that includes a collective defence clause, Al Jazeera reported. The agreement, called the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, passed on Thursday with 279 votes in favour and 119 against, with 398 of the chamber's 592 lawmakers taking part. Turkey signed it in August and sent it to parliament last month.

According to a document seen by Reuters, the pact has 16 articles. Article 1 says the signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity. Article 2 says that if a party faces armed attack, the others shall "immediately provide assistance". Al Jazeera notes this mirrors Article 5 of the NATO treaty. Other articles cover defence industry cooperation, joint training, technological innovation and sharing logistics and intelligence. Members commit for 10 years, and other countries may join with existing members' approval. Syria's government has expressed interest.

Because Turkey belongs to both NATO and the Mecca pact, critics have raised questions about a possible conflict of interest in allocating its military resources. Turkish officials have dismissed those concerns as unfounded.

The vote comes as the Iran-backed Houthis continue attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia said on Thursday it intercepted a drone near Medina. Riyadh has accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca and Medina, which the group rejects.

Al Jazeera says ratification does not guarantee Turkish troops will go to Saudi Arabia, and experts say a deployment would need other legislative steps. Defence Minister Yasar Guler said in October that the scope of support would be set after ratification. Turkish media quoted him as saying Turkey does not foresee entering any conflict with the Houthis and that its support would strengthen deterrence.

The United Nations has condemned the seizure of eight Palestinian homes by Israeli settlers in Jericho in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera reported. UN Secretary-General spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters on Thursday that settlers reportedly "used live ammunition" during the takeover on Wednesday, physically assaulted residents and threw stones, prompting families to flee.

Dujarric said some displaced people now lack adequate shelter, and that the Israeli military has since declared the area a closed military zone, preventing humanitarian workers from reaching them. Peace Now, an Israeli settlement watchdog, said about 30 settlers took over the houses in Ein a-Duyuk a-Tahta on Wednesday afternoon. It said that, according to reports, they assaulted and robbed two Israeli activists and shot a Palestinian man in the leg.

The two sides differ on the legality of the move. The settlers say they legally purchased the homes. Hanan Greenwood, a settler representative, told AFP that Nachala, a right-wing organisation that funds new settlements and campaigns for annexation, bought the homes "with our help". Jericho governor Hussein Hamayel told AFP the land belongs to the Palestinian Authority and cannot be sold, calling the sale documents a forgery.

The land lies in Area C, which has been under Israeli control since the Oslo Accords. Israel has occupied the West Bank since 1967, and more than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements there, which are illegal under international law.

Al Jazeera says settler attacks have approached all-time highs this year and several communities around Jericho have already been driven out. Residents fear the new settlers will escalate attacks and bring a heavier military presence, as, Peace Now says, happened in Hebron, where it described constant friction, restrictions on movement and the displacement of thousands of Palestinians.

Meta, Google and TikTok have each sued California Attorney General Rob Bonta to try to block a law restricting social media features it deems addictive for users under 16, TechCrunch reported. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill, AB 1709, in September, and it takes effect at the start of the new year.

The law bars platforms from offering autoplay videos and personalized feeds to under-16 users, and requires them to delete those users' accounts if the features are not turned off. Platforms that do not comply could face fines of up to $50,000 per affected user under 16.

Meta argues the law violates the First Amendment by overriding its editorial decisions and says Section 230 preempts it. TikTok and Google made similar arguments. Meta wrote that the law would make it unlawful to disseminate speech to minors unless it changes its practices. A TikTok spokesperson called it a "blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression". Google noted that YouTube autoplay is off for minors by default and said parents are best positioned to decide for their families.
Bonta's office said it is reviewing the filings and is committed to "defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online."

Digital safety experts often caution that such laws can compromise privacy for all users by requiring age verification that collects more data. Rindala Alajaji of the Electronic Frontier Foundation said the law compels platforms to collect more information from every user and called it a functional ban on social media for under-16s.

TechCrunch says the suits come as platforms face similar fights elsewhere. Australia banned social media for under-16s in December 2025, while France passed a similar law that its top court struck down over free expression concerns. Meta also agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle children's safety claims from 29 states.

Palo Alto Networks is in talks to acquire Clutch Security, a startup that secures AI agents' access to company systems, for $500 million in cash plus milestone-based payouts, TechCrunch reported, citing a person familiar with the discussions. The Information first reported the talks. Neither company responded to a request for comment.

Clutch is three years old. According to TechCrunch's source, it was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire. It is approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue, so the price would be about 50 times that figure.

TechCrunch says the valuation fits a market focused on defending software against attackers using AI. It noted that Upwind, a cloud security startup, recently turned down a Datadog offer valuing it at roughly 40 times annual recurring revenue.

If completed, the deal would be Palo Alto Networks' seventh acquisition this year, according to PitchBook. The company has a history of buying rather than building and has stepped up dealmaking in response to rising AI-driven cyberattacks. In September it bought Console, an AI help desk startup, valued at $500 million in stock and cash. Other purchases this year include Embrace for $325 million, Chronosphere for $2.95 billion and Koi for $231 million, according to regulatory filings.

Rivals of Clutch have also been acquired. Cyera, valued at $12 billion earlier this year, bought Oasis Security, which also manages AI agents' access to systems, for $1 billion. Cisco bought Astrix for roughly $400 million, Calcalist reported.

A decade-old vulnerability nicknamed *sshole lets attackers log into some devices running Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, without a password, Ars Technica reported. It arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that Alpine uses. OpenSSH using musl must also not use PAM, the framework that handles user authentication.

Exploitation needs two more conditions. The system must have at least one user account reachable with a password hashed using SHA256 or SHA512, and the target account must be passwordless, marked with a "*" in the password field of /etc/shadow. Such accounts are common for certificate-based authentication. When these are met, an attacker can get in by entering more than 256 characters in the password field. Alpine maintainers said that anyone who can reach the SSH port can log in "with one connection, works every time, and needs no retries." Security firm Checkpoint said root accounts are safe under the default PermitRootLogin setting, though reachable accounts with sudo or doas rights can still become root.

Ars Technica says many systems could be exposed. The Alpine Docker Hub base image has more than 1 billion downloads, and Alpine is common in routers, smart TVs and industrial controllers, many hard to update. Detectify said Shodan lists around 22 million systems with SSH open on port 22.

Responsibility is disputed. OpenSSH, which issued an update Thursday, said the root cause is outside sshd but can be avoided there. Musl developer Rich Felker said it is not a musl bug but erroneous use by the caller, and that musl plans changes in an upcoming release. Alpine has also issued an update.

Other affected software is unclear. The discoverer said OpenWRT is affected, though it uses Dropbear by default, and named buildroot and yocto, which are unconfirmed. There is no known CVE designation. Ars Technica advises users of musl with OpenSSH to investigate and install the Alpine and OpenSSH patches.

Blue Origin announced two upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, aimed at cutting manufacturing cost and increasing payload capacity to geostationary orbit and the Moon, Ars Technica reported. CEO Dave Limp spoke at the UP.Summit conference in Florida, saying there has "never been higher demand for launch, ever." The company aims eventually to position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.

The first upgrade is a new engine, Northstar, which Blue Origin has begun test firing and which will eventually replace the BE-4 on New Glenn's first stage. Limp described it as a simplified, more powerful BE-4, with half the parts, 30 percent less mass and about 65 percent 3D-printable. Blue Origin believes it can build it at 25 percent of a BE-4's cost and eventually assemble one in under a day. The BE-4 has 640,000 pounds of thrust; Northstar will start at 715,000. Blue Origin will keep making BE-4s for United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket.

The second is a hydrogen-oxygen third stage called GS3, powered by the BE-7 engine already used in its lunar landers. According to Blue Origin, a GS3-equipped 7x2 New Glenn can carry 8 metric tons directly to geostationary orbit and 10 to translunar injection, rising to 14 and 20 tons for the larger 9x4 variant.

The stage uses lightweight composite tanks, which posed a risk because hydrogen leaks easily and cracking can worsen losses. Limp said the company was unsure a 5.5-meter composite tank could hold hydrogen at high pressure. In Texas, a tank was pressurized to 100 percent of expected maximum for 2.5 hours and 150 percent for 10 minutes. Blue Origin is now aiming for a 2028 debut for a government customer.

At least 10 local governments and police departments have moved since summer to curb, restrict or end their use of Flock Safety technology, TechCrunch reported, as concern grows over mass surveillance and data privacy. Flock sells license plate readers, drones and microphone-based devices that detect gunshots. More than 100,000 of its cameras are in use nationwide.

In the past three months, Monroe, Ohio; Newburgh, New York; Richmond, Virginia; Hopkinton and New Bedford, Massachusetts; and Lansing, Michigan, have moved to end contracts. Police in East Bridgewater and Grafton, Massachusetts, announced plans to stop use. This week, League City, Texas, residents voted against continued use, and the cameras are set to be removed. Earlier, Asheville, North Carolina, terminated its contract, and the El Paso County Sheriff's Office in Colorado said it would stop. Sheriff Joseph Roybal said the office can catch criminals without Flock.

Reasons include privacy, data sharing and procurement. Officers in Missouri and Texas were accused or convicted of using Flock to stalk former partners. Ithaca, New York, cited reports that federal agents, including ICE and ATF, used Flock data without local authorization.

Flock said police use its technology to solve serious crimes and find missing people, and that removing it "moves public safety backward." It said customers own and control their data, that it does not sell data and that it has no contract with ICE. In August it cut the default retention period for new customers from 30 days to seven and began requiring a case code for searches.

Adam Schwartz of the Electronic Frontier Foundation said police often adopt Flock with little council oversight and that many councils are listening to activists. TechCrunch notes that many governments are adding restrictions or seeking alternatives rather than dropping the technology, while Florida barred plate readers from state highways and Texas paused state funding.

Airbnb said in its third-quarter shareholder letter on Thursday that it will launch its own AI travel agent in the first half of 2027, TechCrunch and The Verge reported. The company had previously said only that an agent would arrive within the next year.

Airbnb says the agent will not be a conventional chatbot. CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that planning a trip is different from routine tasks like booking a restaurant, citing a figure that 80 percent of travelers enjoy researching trips. He said general-purpose agents are not the best tool for that. Instead, the agent will draw on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components, including maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries, and compose them in real time around a user's question. Chesky likened it to generative UI.

The company said the agent will help guests explore options, decide with the people they travel with and take action directly in Airbnb. It also plans for the agent to help during a trip, including changing reservations, resolving payment problems, handling refunds and rebooking, and providing 24-hour safety support, which Airbnb says an outside agent cannot easily do. Over time it expects the agent to cover services and experiences as well as homes and hotels.

The announcement came with strong earnings. Revenue grew 19 percent to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates, and Airbnb raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast to the high teens from the mid-teens. Chesky said it was the company's fastest revenue growth in more than three years. In the letter, Airbnb also called AI "the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb."
